## Subqueries in WHERE

A subquery is a query in brackets inside another query. It runs to hand the outer query a list, a yes or no, or one value. Three forms cover most questions.

### IN: a list

`WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_lines WHERE promo_id IS NOT NULL)` keeps each product whose ID is in the list. A product that appears in the list 500 times is still kept once: IN tests membership, it does not join. A join to `order_lines` would repeat the product once per line.

### EXISTS and NOT EXISTS: is there a matching row?

`WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM competitor_prices cp WHERE cp.product_id = p.product_id)` is true when at least one check of that product exists. This subquery is correlated: its WHERE links it to the outer row through the outer alias `p`, so it is worked out again for each product. What it selects does not matter; `SELECT 1` is the habit. NOT EXISTS keeps the rows with no match: products never checked, promotions no line carried.

### NOT IN and missing values

`x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`. The last test is unknown, never true, so the filter keeps no rows at all. `order_lines.promo_id` is missing on every line sold without a promotion, so `promo_id NOT IN (SELECT promo_id FROM order_lines)` finds nothing, even when unused promotions exist. Use NOT EXISTS, or add `WHERE promo_id IS NOT NULL` inside the brackets. Plain IN is safe.

### A scalar subquery: one value

`WHERE unit_cost_eur > (SELECT AVG(unit_cost_eur) FROM products)` compares each row with one number. A subquery used as one value must return at most one row; when it returns two, DuckDB stops with "More than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression". So before you write one, ask: is the column I look up by unique in that table? `product_id` is not unique in `price_history`, which keeps a row per price version, so a price lookup needs `valid_to IS NULL` or an aggregate such as MAX. Data with one match today can have two tomorrow: two products tied at a top price break `= (SELECT product_id ...)`.

### Correlated: the right group

To compare a product with its own category, link an inner copy of the table to the outer row: `(SELECT AVG(p2.unit_cost_eur) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id)`. Give the inner table its own alias, and link on the column the question compares by: `p2.brand = p.brand` would compare with the brand instead. Without the outer alias, `category_id = category_id` compares the inner column with itself, and every product meets every other. Check one row by hand: the subquery's value for it should be its own group's.

### Which form?

- A list to keep or drop: IN, or EXISTS.
- Rows with no match: NOT EXISTS, or a LEFT JOIN and IS NULL.
- One number to compare with: a scalar subquery, with an aggregate or a unique match.
syntax_md:
```sql
SELECT p.product_id, p.unit_cost_eur              -- metrics
FROM products p                                    -- source: one row per product
WHERE p.unit_cost_eur > (                          -- row filter: one value per outer row
  SELECT AVG(p2.unit_cost_eur)                     --   one number
  FROM products p2                                 --   an inner copy with its own alias
  WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id             --   the link to the outer row
);
```

- `col IN (SELECT key FROM ...)`: keep the rows whose value is in the list.
- `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE inner.key = outer.key)`: keep the rows with a match; NOT EXISTS keeps the rows with none.
- A subquery used as one value returns at most one row: aggregate it, or look up by a unique column.
- Never use NOT IN over a column that can be missing.
dialect_note: IN, EXISTS and subqueries in WHERE are standard SQL and read the same in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and BigQuery. DuckDB (checked on 1.5.6) stops with "More than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression" when a subquery used as one value returns two rows, and PostgreSQL stops with an error too. NOT IN finding nothing when its list holds a missing value is not a DuckDB quirk: it follows from how SQL compares with a missing value.

worked_examples.title: Promotions above the average of their type
worked_examples.prompt: Which promotions give a bigger discount than the average discount of the promotions of the same promo_type? Return promo_id, promo_type and discount_pct.

clauses.why: The promotion, its type and its own discount.
One row per promotion; pr is the outer alias the subquery links to.
Each promotion is compared with one number, an average, so the subquery returns one row.
The inner copy of the table gets its own alias, pr2, so the two copies can be told apart.
The link: for each outer promotion, the average covers the promotions of its own type only.

worked_examples.title: Categories with no 2025 launch
worked_examples.prompt: Which categories had no product launched in 2025? Return category_id and category_name.

clauses.why: The category and its name, once per category.
One row per category, including a category whose products all launched earlier.

clauses.text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p
clauses.why: Keep a category when the inner query finds no row at all.
Link each product to the outer category, so only that category's products are searched.

clauses.text: AND p.launch_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-12-31')
clauses.why: Only a 2025 launch counts as a match; NOT EXISTS never trips over a missing value.

why_clause.stem: Why does the subquery need the line WHERE pr2.promo_type = pr.promo_type?

options.text: It ties the average to the outer promotion's type, so each promotion is compared with its own type.
Without it the subquery returns one row per promotion, and the query stops with an error.
It removes the promotions whose promo_type is missing before the average is taken.
It makes the subquery run once for the whole query instead of once per promotion.

why_clause.explanation: The link reads the outer row's promo_type, so for each promotion the average covers only the promotions of that type. Without it the subquery still returns one row, the average of every promotion, and answers a different question. It filters nothing out of the outer query, and a correlated subquery is worked out again for each outer row, not once.
